source.title: Scaling Offline Model-Based RL via Jointly-Optimized World-Action Model Pretraining
source.authors: Jie Cheng; Rui-Xi Qiao; Gang Xiong; Qing-Hai Miao; Yingwei Ma; Bin-Hua Li; Yong-Bin Li; Yi-Sheng Lv

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study explores an analogous scaling trend in visual offline reinforcement learning and reports results across model sizes, but it does not test language-model cross-entropy scaling or fit the power laws in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper cites language-model scaling laws as motivation and measures Atari task returns, not held-out language-model cross-entropy. It does not sweep training tokens or compute, fit loss power laws, or test prediction from smaller runs. Its Atari performance-scaling results are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Kaplan et al. only as motivation. It reports Atari game returns (IQM human- or DQN-normalized score) for three model sizes (40M, 70M, 150M). It reports no held-out loss, fits no power law, varies neither tokens nor compute, and makes no extrapolation. The returns-vs-size trend is a related construct, not a test of any version, including V5, which requires the power-law form. T3 is a testing tranche and does not fit, so this is T6 with relation 'discusses'.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that JOWA's IQM performance on the 15 pretrained games rises with model size, with the steepest curve among the methods compared. The rise is slower without planning. The size trend persists after fine-tuning on 5 unseen games. They note that some individual games run against the trend and that the Zaxxon 'emergence' comes from the reward metric.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures offline RL game returns across model sizes; it does not use the language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling-law recipe or fit loss curves.
record.method_sensitivity: Planning changes aggregate scores and the apparent size trend; the authors also report that raw performance on some games runs against the aggregate trend. Transfer scores vary with fine-tuning data quality.

fits_no_version.finding: The appendix discusses an apparent 'emergent' jump on Zaxxon for JOWA-150M. The authors attribute it to a nonlinear reward: with rewards clipped, scores are 0.08 (70M) vs 0.44 (150M), and they call it no true emergence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Apparent emergent jumps in RL agent scores can arise from nonlinear reward metrics rather than true capability discontinuities.

fits_no_version.finding: The Limitations section states that raw scores in some individual games fall as parameters increase, against the aggregate IQM trend.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In offline multi-game RL, aggregate gains with model size can hide per-task reversals.

record.problems: The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the scaling comparisons. It states that individual-game raw scores sometimes oppose the aggregate trend. The scaling measurements are Atari returns, not loss, and do not establish a power-law relationship.

untested.parts: No loss, no power-law fit, no token or compute sweep; only 3 model sizes.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
Depth and width vary with size; there is no fixed-parameter shape comparison.
The setting is non-text (visual offline RL), but no power-law form is fitted to loss or to performance.
Atari returns rise with size, but the models are not language models and no predictive fit is made.
No exponents or fitting choices are analysed.

missing.what: Figure 2 baseline scaling curves: MTBC (34M/65M/120M) and MGDT (40M/200M). The authors say JOWA shows the steepest curve.

record.verdict_notes: The record's tranche T3 contradicts its own 'not tested' verdicts, so it is changed to T6. There are only three size points and no uncertainty estimates. Rows r1–r3 and r13–r15 duplicate r7–r9, and r2 (0.485) differs from r8 (47.6%), which needs checking.

versions.untested_parts: No language-model held-out pretraining loss, token or compute scaling, or loss power-law fits.
No predictions of larger-run loss from fits on smaller runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep over parameters and tokens.
No controlled comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count for language-model loss.
The study uses visual Atari observations and offline RL, but does not measure whether the claimed power-law form holds for loss in those settings.
It evaluates Atari game returns across model sizes, not predictable downstream language-task performance or performance as a function of pretraining loss.
No language-model scaling-law exponents, fitting choices, or departures from a single loss power law are analyzed.

relation.reason: The introduction and section 5.4 discuss scaling laws as motivation and interpret increasing returns as scaling, without testing the catalog's specified laws or using a fitted law as a tool.

tranche.reason: The paper measures aggregate Atari returns across three sizes, without fitting or testing a power law, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or predictive downstream relationship. This related size trend does not test the specified claim versions.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is arXiv v4 dated 29 January 2026, published at ICLR 2025. Preserve the unresolved JOWA-70M discrepancy: Table 2 gives 48.5%, whereas Table 4 and section 5.3 give 47.6%.
